plain.en: the share of a group that had the exposure

means.en: In a case-control table, the share exposed among the cases, a/(a+c), or among the controls, b/(b+d). Each rate divides by its own column total. For example, if 14 of 20 cases smoked, the exposure rate in the cases is 70 per cent. The number of controls the investigator chooses does not change it.

plain.en: unlikely to be chance

means.en: A result small enough that chance alone would rarely produce it. The usual cut-off is a P value below 0.05, and it says nothing about whether the comparison was fair.

plain.en: the chance of a gap this big by luck

means.en: The chance of seeing a gap at least as large as the one observed if exposure and disease had no link. A shuffle test shows it: deal the same people into the two groups at random many times, and count how often chance alone gives a gap this big. If 3 of 100 shuffles do, the P value is about 0.03. It measures chance only, never bias and never causation.

plain.en: dealing the same people into the groups at random, to see what chance alone gives

means.en: A way to find a P value. Keep every person and their exposure, deal them at random into groups of the same sizes as the real ones, and work out the gap again. Repeat many times: the share of shuffles with a gap at least as big as the real one is the P value. Also called a permutation test.

plain.en: a ratio of two odds

means.en: The odds of exposure among the cases divided by the odds among the controls, ad/bc. It estimates the relative risk fairly only when the disease is rare.

plain.en: risk in the exposed divided by risk in the unexposed

means.en: A ratio of two incidences, so it needs a cohort followed forward. A case-control study cannot measure it directly and reports an odds ratio instead.

plain.en: a third factor linked to both the exposure and the disease

means.en: A factor, such as smoking in a study of alcohol and oesophageal cancer, that is linked to the exposure, is itself a cause of the disease, and is more common in one group than the other. It can create the whole apparent effect. Matching cases and controls on it removes the distortion.

plain.en: picking controls to be like the cases on one factor

means.en: Choosing the controls so that a factor such as smoking or age is spread the same way among the controls as among the cases, so that factor can no longer explain a difference. Group matching evens out the share in each group; pair matching gives each case its own similar control. Never match on the exposure being tested.

plain.en: new cases over a set time among people at risk

means.en: The number of new cases in a period divided by the population at risk. A case-control study cannot measure it, because it never follows a group forward.

plain.en: a systematic error built into the study

means.en: An error created by how the groups were chosen or questioned, not by chance. It pushes the estimate in one direction, and no sample size or P value repairs it.

plain.en: cases remember their past harder

means.en: People with the disease search their memory for the exposure more carefully than people without it, so exposed cases are over-counted and the odds ratio climbs.

plain.en: the questioner digs harder into one group

means.en: An interviewer who knows the hypothesis probes the cases' answers more searchingly than the controls' and records more exposure among the cases. Comparing interview lengths is a direct check.

plain.en: the door into the study picks a tilted sample

means.en: The chosen cases and controls stop representing the populations they came from, because the door that let them in (hospital admission, employment records) admits different kinds of people at different rates.

plain.en: the hospital door manufactures an association

means.en: When the exposure and the disease each raise the chance of hospital admission, the hospital's own patients can show an association that the population behind the hospital does not have. No matching removes it.

plain.en: a group that shares one experience in one period

means.en: A group of people who share one characteristic or experience within a defined time period - all born in 2010, all exposed to one drug, all married in the same year. A cohort study follows such a group forward to count who falls ill.

plain.en: a study that starts before the outcomes have happened

means.en: A cohort study whose investigation begins while the disease outcomes still lie ahead, so it watches them occur. The chapter also calls it a 'current' cohort study.

plain.en: a study that starts after the outcomes are already on record

means.en: A cohort study whose outcomes have all occurred before the investigation begins. The investigator goes back in time, sometimes 10 to 30 years, picks the groups from old employment, medical or other records, and traces them forward to the present; also called a 'historical' cohort study.

plain.en: people slipping out of a study while it runs

means.en: The loss of study members during follow-up, through death, moving away or refusal to continue. A cohort is practical when attrition can be minimised, because every loss thins the denominators the analysis needs.

plain.en: a disease of the spine

means.en: A painful condition in which the joints of the spine stiffen. Between 1934 and 1954 it was often treated with large doses of radiation therapy, which is how the Court-Brown and Doll cohort could be picked out of treatment records years later.

plain.en: a heart attack

means.en: A heart attack: a patch of heart muscle dies when its blood supply is cut off. Everyone who survived one in a particular year can form a cohort.

plain.en: the death of a newborn baby

means.en: The death of a baby in the weeks around the birth. It was the outcome counted in the Boston foetal-monitoring study, and it follows each birth within days or weeks.

plain.en: a cancer of gland-forming lining cells

means.en: A cancer that starts in the cells of a lining that make secretions. In the Boston cluster it appeared in the lining of the vagina, in women far younger than usual.

plain.en: a synthetic oestrogen, DES

means.en: A man-made oestrogen once given in early pregnancy to prevent miscarriage. The Boston case-control study linked it to vaginal cancer in the daughters 10 to 20 years later.

plain.en: looking at tissue under a microscope

means.en: The study of tissue under a microscope. A case confirmed by histology has had a sample of the tumour examined, so the diagnosis does not rest on symptoms alone.

plain.en: matching on too much

means.en: Matching cases and controls on too many things, or on something the exposure itself changes, so that suitable controls are hard to find and the real difference is pulled toward nothing.

plain.en: a blood clot in a vein, often deep in the leg

means.en: A clot that forms inside a vein and blocks it. In young women it is rare; a piece that breaks off can travel to the lungs.

plain.en: a clot that has travelled to the lungs

means.en: A clot, usually from a leg vein, that lodges in an artery of the lung. It can kill.

plain.en: a rare cancer of blood-vessel lining

means.en: A cancer of the cells that line blood vessels. Angiosarcoma of the liver is very rare, so a cluster of cases in one workplace stands out.

plain.en: the gas PVC plastic is made from

means.en: An industrial gas turned into PVC plastic. Men who cleaned the tanks breathed high doses of it.

plain.en: a cancer of the blood-forming cells

means.en: A cancer of the cells in the bone marrow that make blood cells. Radiation is one of its known causes.

plain.en: the study of disease in groups of people

means.en: The study of how often a disease occurs in groups of people and what causes it. Its studies compare groups, not single patients.

plain.en: a study that starts from the sick and looks back

means.en: A study that starts from people who have the disease (cases) and similar people who do not (controls), and compares how often each group had the exposure in the past.
